newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss court rejects bid by local Anne Frank fund.
newsitem.headline: Swiss court rejects bid by local Anne Frank fund.

text.p: Switzerland's highest court on Thursday reached a decision on the right to commercially use the name of Anne Frank, the young Dutch diarist murdered by the Nazis in 1945, but the legal battle is not yet over.
The court rejected a request by the Anne Frank Fund in Basel to dismiss a competing trademark application filed by an Amsterdam institution bearing nearly the same name.

Legal experts said the ruling by the Federal Tribunal in Lausanne means the Anne Frank Foundation in Amsterdam may charge license fees for souvenirs sold in Switzerland using the wartime Jewish diarist's name -- which the Basel Fund wants to prevent.
The Basel fund, which owns the copyright to Anne's best-selling diary found at her wartime hiding place in Amsterdam, was set up by her father Otto Heinrich Frank in 1963.

"We are the sole heir to Otto and Anne Frank. We don't want any commercialisation of her name -- no t-shirts or coffee mugs," Bernhard 'Buddy' Elias, a first cousin of Anne Frank who serves as director of the small Basel fund, told Reuters.
He declined any comment on the legal dispute in Switzerland.
Otto Frank survived Auschwitz and moved in with his own sister, Elias' mother, in Basel after World War Two. His first wife Edith and other daughter Margot also died at Bergen-Belsen death camp.
"We were his family after the war," Elias said.
Otto Frank died in 1980 at Bielfelden, near Basel.
The high court upheld a Zurich commercial court ruling which recognised a 1993 trademark registration application for Switzerland filed by the Anne Frank Foundation in Amsterdam.
The Federal Tribunal ruled that under the circumstances, the Dutch-based foundation benefitted from a priority of rights beause it had been the first to file for trademark protection.
But the high court did not address a trademark application filed by the Basel fund in 1994, meaning the final chapter in the awkward legal battle is still to be written.
Oscar Battegay, the Basel fund's lawyer, told Reuters: "The Anne Frank Fund wants to prevent anybody from commercialising the trade mark.
"The Federal Tribunal dismissed an action by the Anne Frank Fund that asked that the trademark registration of the Amsterdam organisation be declared null and void.
"There is a final and binding decision concerning the registration of trade mark of the Amsterdam foundation, but not yet one concerning the application of the Anne Frank Fund."
"That's the next step," the lawyer added.
The Swiss Federal Intellectual Property Office will decide on the Basel trade mark application, whose ultimate fate is also likely to lie in the hands of Swiss courts.
The Basel fund owns the copyright to Anne Frank's diary which has been translated worldwide, selling 26 million copies.
Elias said all of the fund's diary proceeds were donated to charities representing his late cousin's humanitarian ideals -- "unification of mankind, helping children and peace projects".
Battegay put the Funds' assets at 10 million swiss francs (6.6 million dollars). It expected to give 250,000-300,000 swiss francs to charities in 1997.
